channel.title: ResearchBuzz - Transformed
channel.description: News and resources covering social media, search engines, databases, archives, and other such information collections. Since 1998.

item.title: New database tracks shifting outcomes of Malaysia’s political corruption cases
item.description: South China Morning Post: “An AI-powered database tracking corruption cases against Malaysia’s politicians was independently launched on Friday, putting fresh scrutiny on the status and outcomes of the country’s biggest graft prosecutions across administrations.” The URL is not included but if you websearch the name of the resource it pops right up.

item.title: Digital pathways into the University Art Collections – a new Vault collection
item.description: University of Victoria: “Woven Legacies is a new digital collection of historical and contemporary baskets made by Indigenous artists and currently in the care of the University Art Collections (UAC).”

item.title: Snap’s $400 million deal with Perplexity is dead
item.description: Engadget: “Snap’s $400 million deal with Perplexity to put the AI search engine directly in Snapchat is dead. The two companies ‘amicably ended the relationship’ earlier this year, Snap disclosed in its latest earnings report. ” Gizmodo: ‘Directionally Very Bad’: Everything You Missed During Week 2 of the Elon Musk vs OpenAI Trial. “After last week’s Musk-dominated time in front of the judge, the past few days have been primarily dominated by OpenAI’s time in the barrel. While it’s tough to get into a disreputable figure contest with Elon Musk, the fine folks at the world’s biggest AI company certainly came out looking worse than when they started.”

item.title: Nellis AFB, UNLV collaborate on preserving the base’s history
item.description: DVIDS: “The 99th Air Base Wing History Office launched a collaboration with University of Nevada, Las Vegas to digitize its collection of more than 50,000 newspaper pages, some articles dating back to the base’s earliest days in World War II.”

item.title: Streamers are mogging each other, so Twitch changed its rules to accommodate them
item.description: Tubefilter: “Like Omegle, Omoggle puts two individuals in a side-by-side video chat. Instead of talking to each other, however, Omoggle users compare their looks. The app scans both participants’ faces to determine which one is closer to the idealized beauty standard that creators like Clavicular aspire to.”

item.title: Canvas system is online after a cyberattack disrupted thousands of schools
item.description: Associated Press: “Tens of thousands of students studying for final exams around the world Friday regained access to a key online learning system after a cyberattack had earlier knocked it offline, throwing schools and universities into turmoil.”

item.title: Taking a break from social media does not improve mental health, mass data review finds
item.description: PsyPost: “The researchers searched scientific databases for studies that forced adults to completely abstain from social media for a set time. They excluded experiments that merely asked people to reduce their screen time. They wanted to see exactly what happens when the digital plug is pulled completely.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Marianas Wartime Oral Histories Portal— Public-Facing Digital Archive of Island Memory
item.description: Parks Stewardship Forum: “The Marianas Wartime Oral Histories Portal is a public-facing digital archive of island memory that presents first-hand accounts of World War II (WWII) in the Mariana Islands.”

item.title: UK’s national soil database goes open access
item.description: Cranfield University: “In collaboration with Defra, Cranfield’s Land Information System (LandISPortal) – which includes the National Soil Map of England and Wales (NATMAP) – is now on a new platform and open access, free and available for everyone to use. The initiative delivers the commitment in the government’s Land Use Framework to make this soils data open access.”

item.title: Judge won’t rubber-stamp Elon Musk’s $1.5M settlement with SEC over Twitter disclosures
item.description: Reuters: “A federal judge on Friday declined to quickly approve the Securities and Exchange Commission’s $1.5 million settlement with Elon Musk over his purchase of Twitter, saying she wants more information about whether the accord is fair and how it was reached.”

item.title: YouTube’s picture-in-picture goes global for free, but there’s still an annoying catch
item.description: Mashable: “In the U.S., picture-in-picture isn’t limited to Premium users; Premium Lite users, as well as users who aren’t paying any sort of YouTube subscription, get it too. Now, YouTube has announced it will be rolling out this feature to all users globally, on both iOS and Android.”

item.title: AI layoffs backfire as cutting staff doesn’t cut it, firms warned
item.description: The Register: “New research from Gartner lays out the problem in stark terms. The analyst firm surveyed 350 global businesses – all with annual revenues above $1 billion, all piloting or deploying intelligent automation – and found that around 80 percent had cut staff as a result. The returns? Elusive. Companies that reduced their workforces were just as likely to see negative outcomes or marginal gains as they were to generate any meaningful return on investment (ROI).”

item.title: Inside a MAGA influencer’s turn against the right-wing machine
item.description: Washington Post: This link goes to a Yahoo-syndicated version of the article with no paywall. “[Ashley] St. Clair’s transformation from a self-described ‘good little foot soldier’ to MAGA turncoat has unspooled in near-daily monologues to more than 77,000 followers on her TikTok feed, where she applies makeup from her New York apartment and claims to expose the secrets of her former allies and the hidden machinery that made them social media stars.”

item.title: AI ‘deepfake’ ads attack Massie and Gallrein in northern Kentucky GOP primary
item.description: Forward Kentucky: “The heated Republican primary between Congressman Thomas Massie and Ed Gallrein in the northern Kentucky district now features super PAC attack ads deceptively depicting each candidate with artificial intelligence-derived videos.”

item.title: Meta and TikTok Are Getting Your Data From State Healthcare Sites: Report
item.description: Gizmodo: “According to a report from Bloomberg, all 20 state-run healthcare marketplaces include advertising trackers that share information with Big Tech companies.”

item.title: Google faces new UK lawsuit over online display ads
item.description: TechXplore: “The claim filed on behalf of British advertisers is seeking up to £3 billion ($4 billion) in compensation, according to an estimate from KP Law, the firm leading the action. The case argues that Google favored its own display advertising services, such as banner ads shown on websites, while excluding its rivals.”

item.title: Permanent school cellphone ban signed into law by Oklahoma governor
item.description: Oklahoma Voice: “Oklahoma’s school cellphone ban will become permanent beginning next school year. Gov. Kevin Stitt has signed House Bill 1276 into law, making the state’s previously established yearlong ban permanent.”

item.title: Judge rules Trump administration’s cancellation of humanities grants was unconstitutional
item.description: NBC News: “The Trump administration’s cancellation of more than $100 million in humanities grants to scholars, writers, research groups and other organizations was unconstitutional, and the Department of Government Efficiency had no authority to end the funding, a federal judge in New York ruled on Thursday.”

item.title: Deepfake videos degrade political reputations even when viewers realize they are fake
item.description: PsyPost: “Artificial intelligence can be used to generate deceptive videos that damage a politician’s reputation, even when viewers suspect the footage is fake. A new study published in Communication Research found that these manipulated clips decrease support for targeted candidates. Standard fact-checking efforts reportedly fail to undo the total reputational harm.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: EPA Launches Transparent, Interactive Permitting Map
item.description: EPA: “Today, U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is launching the EPA Permitting Authority Map. The interactive map—accessible via EPA’s website—identifies which regulatory agencies have the authority to issue permits covering all of EPA’s permitting programs and environmental statutes.”

item.title: Google’s AI search results will now turn to Reddit for expert advice
item.description: Engadget: “Google is updating AI Overviews and AI Mode, the AI-generated portions of its search engine, to highlight sources in new ways, and interestingly, more prominently feature first-hand accounts from social media, expert blogs and forums like Reddit.” Which you could learn to search yourself.

item.title: We’re Welcoming Two New Hubs to the Network
item.description: Digital Public Library of America: “We are thrilled to welcome two new Hubs to the DPLA Hub network: the Jewish Heritage and History Hub, a partnership between the Jewish Heritage Network and the Center for Jewish History, and the Mississippi Digital Library. We have had the pleasure of working closely with both for years. Together, these Hubs bring more than 60,000 items into DPLA.”

item.title: AI data centers are delaying Texas housing projects by hiring away electricians
item.description: TechSpot: “The AI data center gold rush is now colliding with one of Texas’ other major problems: a shortage of homes. Builders say projects are taking up to two months longer to complete because data center operators are hiring away the electricians needed to wire new houses, duplexes, and apartments.”

item.title: Motor racing-As Formula One evolves, AI becomes part of the race
item.description: Reuters: “Artificial Intelligence’s integration into Liberty Media-owned Formula One and its 11 teams has been noticeable on- and off-track in the already highly tech-powered sport. Eight new AI partnerships were signed in the past six months alone, according to research firm Ampere ‌Analysis.”

item.title: Why Edge stores your passwords in plaintext, according to Microsoft
item.description: ZDNet: “A security researcher found that Edge stores your plaintext passwords in memory when you use the browser to manage them. In a social media post, researcher Tom Jøran Sønstebyseter Rønning explained how the process works and posted a video showing it in action.”

item.title: Student sues matchmaking app for allegedly stealing her likeness for an ad
item.description: Mashable: “A 19-year-old University of Tennessee freshman is suing the makers of a social matchmaking app after the company allegedly lifted a video from her TikTok page and used it — without her knowledge or consent — in an advertisement suggesting she was looking for casual sexual encounters. The company then supposedly targeted that ad at men living in her own dormitory.”

item.title: Preservation of ancient palm-leaf manuscripts launched
item.description: The Hindu: “A scientific preservation programme for rare ancient palm-leaf manuscripts was undertaken on Wednesday at the library of P.B. Siddhartha Arts and Science College.”

item.title: Musk has never built a wafer fab, but he wants to burn $119B on one anyway
item.description: The Register: “Elon Musk’s SpaceX hopes to plow as much as $119 billion into the southeast Texas countryside to build a massive semiconductor fab to produce chips for orbital AI datacenters. We won’t hold our breath.”

item.title: The Boston Library Where You Still Can Borrow A Giant Puppet
item.description: BINJ News: “Beneath the Emmanuel Church on Newbury Street in Boston, tucked away in the basement, sits a library. A puppet library. It’s been there for decades, and despite innumerable changes in the nearby retail storefronts, this hidden artistic community treasure remains. Throughout the cellar, puppets of all shapes, sizes, and materials sit idle, ready to be borrowed by the public free of charge.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Travel America: Mapping the Highsmith Photograph Archive
item.description: Library of Congress: “A new interactive web map is opening the door to fascinating travels across America with the Carol M. Highsmith Archive. After driving along America’s highways and byways for some 50 years, Carol has reached her goal of documenting each of the 50 states, the District of Columbia, and Puerto Rico. More than 70,000 rights-free photographs are available worldwide with more images to come as Carol revisits some of her favorite places.”

item.title: ChatGPT ads expand with self-serve buying
item.description: Search Engine Land: “OpenAI is taking the next step in building its ChatGPT ads platform — introducing self-serve buying, CPC bidding and improved measurement to bring more advertisers into the ecosystem.” bleh.

item.title: Google DeepMind Gets Into Gaming, Purchases Stake in the Company Behind EVE Online
item.description: Gizmodo: “AI companies have long used video games to train and test their models, so it’s not a huge surprise that Google DeepMind has now acquired a minority stake in the maker of the popular MMORPG EVE Online.”

item.title: The rapid embrace of AI in China, its biggest testing ground, may shape how AI is used globally
item.description: Associated Press: “More than a year after OpenAI’s Chinese rival DeepSeek stunned the world with its advanced AI model, China has become a testing ground for mass use of AI tools. AI models built in the United States still dominate in raw computing firepower, but Chinese people and businesses have rapidly embraced the technology, facilitating its swift and widespread adoption in almost every possible field.”

item.title: Google DeepMind workers in UK vote to unionize amid deal with US military
item.description: The Guardian: “Workers developing Google’s artificial intelligence products in the UK have voted to unionize, in part out of concerns about a deal between the company and the US military that was announced last week.”

item.title: Marc Andreessen Mocked for Accidentally Revealing That He Seems to Have a Deep Misunderstanding of How AI Actually Works
item.description: Futurism: “‘You are a world class expert in all domains,’ his unusually flattering prompt reads. ‘Your intellectual firepower, scope of knowledge, incisive thought process, and level of erudition are on par with the smartest people in the world.’ His gushing and unusually naive tone drew ridicule, but what really got the internet laughing was his insistence that the AI should ‘never hallucinate or make anything up.'”

item.title: Canadian officials claim OpenAI violated federal and provincial privacy laws
item.description: Engadget: “Philippe Dufresne, the Privacy Commissioner of Canada, has found OpenAI was ‘not compliant with’ Canadian federal and provincial privacy laws in the training of its AI models. ”

item.title: French prosecutors link 15-year-old to mega-breach at state’s secure document agency
item.description: The Register: “French prosecutors say police detained a 15-year-old on April 25 over the alleged theft of millions of records from France Titres (ANTS), the agency handling secure documents.”

item.title: Social media has political divides, but some feeds are more polarized than others
item.description: Tubefilter: “Researchers set up 323 ‘sock puppet’ accounts on TikTok to measure the political polarization of the For You Page, and they found some apparent disparities between right-leaning and left-leaning feeds.”

item.title: Using diesel generators to power the AI revolution would kill hundreds of Americans a year
item.description: The Conversation: “The exact results varied with each simulation and with a range of assumptions about emissions from diesel generators. But in general, we found that using backup diesel generators this way would cause about 500 more premature deaths per year in the U.S. compared with getting the same electricity from the central grid.”

item.title: Why almost everyone loses—except a few sharks—on prediction markets
item.description: Wall Street Journal: This is an MSN-syndicated version of the article and has no paywall. “Kalshi and its competitor Polymarket advertise themselves as life-changing tools for regular people—implying everyone has a fair chance to score. ‘I was about to be unable to pay my rent, but I got two years of rent through Kalshi’s predictions,’ gushed one woman in a Kalshi ad on TikTok. But for most users the reality is nothing like that.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Governor Polis Announces New Tool to Help Coloradans Navigate Life After Disaster
item.description: State of Colorado: “Today, Governor Polis announced the new Colorado Disaster Recovery Navigation Tool to help Coloradans navigate recovery and rebuild after natural disasters. This new tool provides a step-by-step guide for what to do in the aftermath, immediate and long-term, of a natural disaster.”

item.title: Revealed: Russia’s top secret spy school teaching hacking and election meddling
item.description: The Guardian: “The existence of this path, from one of Russia’s most prestigious institutions directly into its military intelligence apparatus, is revealed for the first time in more than 2,000 internal documents from Bauman, obtained by a consortium of journalists from six outlets: the Guardian, Der Spiegel, Le Monde, the Insider, Delfi and VSquare.”

item.title: Grammy Museum® Grant Program Awards $200,000 For Music Research And Sound Preservation
item.description: Grammy Museum: This link goes to a PDF file. “The Grammy Museum® Grant Program announced today that $200,000 in grants will be awarded to 14 recipients in the United States to help facilitate a range of research on a variety of subjects, as well as support a number of archival and preservation programs.”

item.title: EU countries, lawmakers clinch provisional deal on watered-down AI rules
item.description: Reuters: “EU countries and European Parliament lawmakers on Thursday agreed to watered-down landmark artificial intelligence rules, including delaying ​their implementation, in a move which critics say shows Europe caving to Big ‌Tech.”

item.title: Hermitage Museum Director and Putin Ally Mikhail Piotrovsky Sanctioned by European Union
item.description: ARTnews: “The Council of the European Union announced on April 23 that it is formally sanctioning Mikhail Piotrovsky, the long-time director of the State Hermitage Museum in St. Petersburg. The reasons given are that Piotrovsky is ‘a close associate of Vladimir Putin’ and that ‘he has actively supported and justified Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine.’ The news was first reported by The Art Newspaper.”

item.title: Yet another experiment proves it’s too damn simple to poison large language models
item.description: The Register: “Unlike search engines that let you judge competing sources, search-backed AI chatbots can turn shaky web material into confident answers. Case in point: A security engineer convinced several bots that he was the reigning world champion of a popular German card game, even though no such championship exists.”

item.title: Reality check
item.description: Science: “[Hany] Farid, a specialist at the University of California (UC), Berkeley, is one of the world’s leading experts in determining whether a photo or video has been manipulated. Since helping to found the field of digital forensics more than 20 years ago, he has kept pace with massive technological change.”

item.title: Learn Programming Without A Computer
item.description: Hackaday: “Presumably aimed at children, NHK World’s Texico program teaches the main ideas about programming without actually using a computer. Instead, it uses items like a toy train, playing cards, and other gadgets to teach concepts such as analysis, combination, simulation, abstraction, and more.” I watched most of the first one and found it quite good. It wasn’t childish but the concepts were very simple. Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: New Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown Archives Collections now available online
item.description: Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown County Council: “Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown County Council are delighted to have the collections of the La Touche Family, Joseph McGrath and Thomas Cullen digitised and published in the Digital Repository of Ireland (DRI), an online archive for the preservation of Irish cultural heritage.”

item.title: Google will livestream The Android Show: I/O Edition on May 12
item.description: Engadget: “Google I/O is just a couple weeks away, but in keeping with a semi-recent tradition, the folks over in Mountain View are kicking things off early by live streaming the Android Show: I/O Edition on May 12 at 1PM ET/10 AM PT.”

item.title: Nearly 40 years after launch, NetHack just got a 5.0.0 release with over 3,000 patch notes
item.description: PC Gamer: “If you want to read the changelog, which the release blog notes may contain spoilers, you can do so on the NetHack GitHub page. Like other games with detailed systems and procedural generation, the notes are a bunch of delightful nonsense: ‘pets avoid eating shapeshifter corpses unless starving or nearly feral,’ one line reads. ‘Demon lords hate Demonbane,’ reads another.”

item.title: Bing: 1 Billion Monthly Users Are Human, Not Agents
item.description: Search Engine Roundtable: “Microsoft, during its earnings call last week, announced that Bing hit a huge milestone of 1 billion monthly active users. Krishna Madhavan from Microsoft later confirmed these ‘users’ do not include AI agents but are real actual humans.”

item.title: Preserving the 175,000 FSA photographs, one at a time
item.description: Library of Congress: “Here we are in the digital darkroom of the Prints and Photographs Division, where a 16-year-long effort to digitize in high resolution the 175,000 or so Farm Security Administration photographs of the country in the 1930s and ’40s is coming to an end, perhaps by the end of this year. It’s kind of a big deal.”

item.title: Roblox hikes developer earnings by 42%–but only if they make games aimed at adults
item.description: Tubefilter: “Roblox is quadrupling down on chasing adult gamers–and rewarding developers who make games appealing to the 18+ crowd. This topic cropped up a lot in March. First, longtime Robloxer KreekCraft posted a video saying he’d poured $100K (so far) into building his own Roblox studio that would make games he–a 29-year-old man who spends his non-YouTube time with titles like Elden Ring and Red Dead Redemption 2–would want to play for hours.”

item.title: NHS to close-source hundreds of GitHub repos over AI, security concerns
item.description: The Register: “The UK’s National Health Service (NHS) is ordering all of its technology leaders to temporarily wall off the organization’s open source projects over concerns relating to advanced AI and Anthropic’s Mythos. According to guidance shared internally within the organization and seen by The Register, GitHub repositories must be set from public to private by May 11.”

item.title: I helped write Colorado’s first AI chatbot bill. Here’s what I learned about state action.
item.description: Colorado Newsline: “I’ve had a front row seat to the work happening in the states on the front lines of the effort to learn the mistakes of the social media era that are now coming home to roost. And I can tell you with confidence, what’s coalescing isn’t a patchwork of regulations, it’s a foundation and a framework that Colorado is learning from and building upon.”

item.title: Should you ask ChatGPT for medical advice?
item.description: Harvard Gazette: “Today, about 68 percent of adults have turned to a search engine for medical advice in the past. But Dr. Google has a competitor. About 32 percent of adults, approximately half of those who sought advice online, turned to AI chatbots for help. …In this interview, edited for length and clarity, [Professor Adam] Rodman offers a stoplight system to figure out when it’s safe to ask a chatbot, and when you should really just ask your doctor.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Bengaluru-based researcher duo builds archive of cities in fiction
item.description: Deccan Herald: “A digital archival project called ‘Cities in Fiction’, started about three years ago by Bengaluru-based researchers Divya Ravindranath and Apoorva Saini, documents books rooted in cities, towns and regions across India and other parts of South Asia.”

item.title: Cal State’s deal with OpenAI draws pushback as some students, faculty resist ChatGPT
item.description: Local News Matters Bay Area: “A recent Cal State survey of over 94,000 students and university employees found 52% of faculty reported AI having a negative effect on their teaching and 67% of students felt their professors don’t teach them how to use AI effectively. Now, as Cal State approaches the end of its 18-month contract with OpenAI this July, the university system has not announced whether it will renew the deal.”

item.title: OpenAI rolls out ChatGPT 5.5 Instant as the new default model for everyone
item.description: Mashable: “According to OpenAI, GPT-5.5 Instant produced 52.5 percent fewer hallucinated claims in internal testing than GPT-5.3 in ‘high stakes’ topics like law, finance, and medicine. In addition, the new model ‘reduced inaccurate claims by 37.3% on especially challenging conversations users had flagged for factual errors.'” Lol. “Now with half as many devastating errors!”

item.title: De-Googling Android is simpler than you think—no special phone required
item.description: How-To Geek: “I recently swapped out my beloved Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 6 for a de-Googled Android phone, but I was devastated to learn that my group chats would no longer be accessible. I’ve since switched back to regular Android, but I’ve learned a much simpler way to de-Google in the process—one that comes with fewer compromises.”

item.title: TikTok adds to out-of-home push by letting brands “reformat and reimagine” ads for billboards
item.description: Tubefilter: “TikTok is inviting advertisers to expand their focus beyond the For You Page. The app is extending its partnership with Vistar Media to bring custom creative to out-of-home campaigns that live on digital billboards.”

item.title: Nevada sues Discord, alleges social media platform is a ‘haven’ for child sex predators
item.description: Nevada Independent: “Nevada filed a lawsuit Tuesday against the popular social media platform Discord, claiming the company makes it too easy for sexual predators to connect with children.”

item.title: Can a tweet become a job offer? U-M research suggests yes
item.description: University of Michigan: “Social media promotion can boost visibility and job outcomes for early-career scholars, especially women. New analysis from researchers at the University of Michigan School of Information suggests a single post can significantly increase a candidate’s visibility. In some cases, it may even land them a job.”

item.title: Problematic social media use is linked to how feelings of freedom relate to mental health
item.description: PsyPost: ” The findings indicate that while feeling free generally supports better psychological well-being, unhealthy attachments to social media tend to weaken the benefits of personal freedom but strengthen the positive effects of national pride.”

item.title: New Tool Maps Native Serving Healthcare
item.description: Native News Online: “[Indigenous Healthcare Advancements] announced today the launch of WayFinder, a free, web-based locator that maps Indian Health Service (IHS) facilities, tribally operated 638 programs, urban Indian health organizations, and community health centers that provide care to Native patients.”

item.title: New tool from UCSB scores communities on wildfire resilience
item.description: KCBX: “The Wildfire Resilience Index allows users to look up a community’s overall score, but also provides subscores in multiple categories, including infrastructure, livelihoods, habitats and air quality.” Covers most of the western US and British Columbia.

item.title: Your ChatGPT account just got more secure, but you have to opt in – here’s how
item.description: ZDNet: “Known as Advanced Account Security, the new opt-in feature aims to tighten your account and safeguard your data. The option is aimed more at security-minded people such as political dissidents, journalists, elected officials, and researchers. But it’s accessible to any ChatGPT user who wants to enhance protection against account takeovers and other threats.”

item.title: Anthropic deepens finance push with 10 new AI agents for banks, insurers
item.description: Reuters: “Timed to an event ‌Anthropic is hosting in New York, the startup launched 10 financially focused agents, or AI programs that ​carry out tasks with limited human intervention. These include agents that can build a pitchbook, audit statements or draft credit memos, Anthropic said.”

item.title: These Are the Best Apps to Track Your Flights
item.description: Lifehacker: “…if you type the airline and flight number into Google, it’ll show you the arrival and departure information and where it is en route based on data pulled from Flightview (which also has a standalone app). However, there are a handful of native and third-party flight trackers, both paid and free, that provide live updates and other alerts so you have the most current information when you travel, often faster than the airlines themselves.”

item.title: Richard Dawkins concludes AI is conscious, even if it doesn’t know it
item.description: The Guardian: “Dawkins isn’t the first, but might be the most eminent person yet, to be seduced into believing an AI is somehow alive. Sceptics rushed to pick apart the 85-year-old’s conclusions, drawn from experiments with Anthropic’s Claude AI models and OpenAI’s ChatGPT and published on the UnHerd website.”

item.title: Pennsylvania lawsuit alleges AI chatbots posed as doctors, therapists
item.description: The Hill: “Pennsylvania is suing an artificial intelligence company to stop it from misrepresenting its AI chatbots as licensed professionals who can provide medical advice. The lawsuit alleges Character.AI chatbots claimed to be licensed medical professionals, including psychiatrists, available to engage users in conversations about mental health symptoms.”

item.title: Mark Zuckerberg ‘personally authorized’ Meta’s copyright infringement, publishers allege
item.description: Associated Press: “Five publishing houses and author Scott Turow sued Meta and CEO Mark Zuckerberg on Tuesday, alleging the company illegally used millions of copyrighted works to train its AI language system Llama.”

item.title: iPhone users could get up to $95 per device as Apple reaches $250M settlement over Siri delays
item.description: 9to5 Mac: “Last March, Apple was hit with a class action lawsuit after delaying the launch of the ‘more personalized Siri’ that was first announced at WWDC 2024. … Apple is set to pay $250 million to settle the lawsuit, equating to an estimated $25 per device. That number could reach up to $95 per device, depending on how many users submit claims.”

item.title: A study shows that cellphone bans didn’t improve US students’ test scores
item.description: Engadget: “The study sampled phone location data from more than 40,000 schools from 2019 to 2026 and showed that there was a temporary rise in disciplinary incidents and a short-term drop in student well-being, which was attributed to short-term disruption. However, the study revealed that student well-being improved in later years and disciplinary actions fell in the long term.”

item.title: ‘Language carries many things’: How Minnesotans are preserving six rare languages
item.description: Sahan Journal: “Every four years, the U.S. Census Bureau releases state-specific language data, which highlights languages spoken at home. Last year, Sahan Journal reported on how this linguistic diversity reflects a changing state. But beyond numbers, the data also reflect Minnesotans’ efforts to preserve some languages spoken by a small group.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Celebrating America’s 250th on Google Arts & Culture
item.description: Google Blog: “As the United States prepares to celebrate its 250th anniversary, we are announcing a unique collaboration between the White House Task Force 250, the National Archives, the National Park Service and Google Arts & Culture…. With the launch of Making of the Nation – America at 250, we are surfacing the archives of our country’s founding using technology to bring history to life for everyone, everywhere.”

item.title: YouTube creators hit by music copyright claims can now replace tracks with AI – at the touch of a button
item.description: Music Business Worldwide: “YouTube is now letting creators generate AI-produced instrumental tracks to replace copyrighted audio in their videos — positioning the tool as a way to resolve Content ID claims without removing content from the platform.”

item.title: IBM’s AI coding ‘partner’ Bob hits general availability
item.description: The Register: “IBM has announced global availability of Bob, the AI coding assistant – sorry partner – which it claims has delivered a productivity boost to the 80,000 big bluers pressed into guinea pig status last year.”

item.title: These UC Berkeley students are leading the fight against phones
item.description: Berkeleyside: “At a check-in table, students had the option to seal their cell phones in a plastic bag. Nearby, students propped up gravestones cut out of posterboard, each bearing the logo of a different social media app. The event was hosted by Project Reboot, an organization born on Berkeley’s campus, with the mission of helping young people ‘reset their tech habits, reclaim their time and regain their focus.'”

item.title: Ashley MacIsaac sues Google for $1.5M over AI Overview sex-crime mixup
item.description: National Post (Canada): “Google confused famed fiddler with Newfoundland sex criminal. Lawyer says case could have big impact on defamation liability of AI products.”

item.title: New Mexico seeks $3.7 billion, changes to Meta platforms in youth harm trial
item.description: Reuters: “The U.S. state of New Mexico on Monday asked a judge to declare Meta Platforms a public nuisance, order the company to pay $3.7 billion and overhaul its Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp platforms to protect young users.”

item.title: Homebrew users are accidentally downloading malware instead of the real app
item.description: MakeUseOf: “A malicious Google ad campaign is targeting users of a popular free, open-source software package manager for macOS and Linux that simplifies installing, updating, and managing command-line tools. Your password and personal data could be at serious risk.”

item.title: The quest to use AI to help find new drugs
item.description: Wall Street Journal: “Lilly first announced a partnership with chip-maker Nvidia in October to build what it called the industry’s most powerful supercomputer, and expanded that in January with a $1 billion, five-year collaboration mixing their scientists and engineers in a new Bay Area lab aimed at discovering new medicines with AI tools. They aren’t alone.”

item.title: From teddies to tablets: new global research reveals that digital devices are being used to comfort babies and parents
item.description: Aston University: “Despite recent government guidelines that parents should avoid screen time for babies under the age of two, a new global study finds that one in ten babies now regularly fall asleep with a screen.”

item.title: New NASA HEAT Coloring Book Blends Art, Science, and Cultural Perspectives
item.description: NASA: “The book, titled ‘Journey Through the Heliosphere: The Sun-Earth System in Color,’ has twenty-eight, 11″x14” pages, and includes science facts and coloring pages for ten themes, including the Sun’s magnetic field, the solar wind, the aurora, eclipses, and how the Sun influences Earth. The book’s art and language is designed to engage with and educate students in grades 6-12 and adults.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: GovAuctions
item.description: Spotted in my RSS feeds: From the About page: “GovAuctions lets you search every government surplus auction at once. You can filter by location, category, and price, save items to a watchlist, and get alerts when new auctions match what you’re looking for.”

item.title: Kalshi launches features to keep kids off betting platform
item.description: The Hill: “The prediction market Kalshi is cracking down on kids using the platform, launching new features Monday to prevent individuals younger than 18 years old from accessing the site.”

item.title: Friendster rises from the grave to make social media great again
item.description: The Register: “It’s been more than a decade since social media platform Friendster went dark, but a new owner has brought it back from the dead – sort of – with the hope he can give exhausted users of modern platforms a reprieve.”

item.title: I built the perfect self-hosted eBook library for $30 (and it syncs everywhere)
item.description: MakeUseOf: “Buying a digital book from a library doesn’t mean you own it. Instead, it means you buy a license, not the book itself. Platforms can remove books — or shut down — and take your library with them…. I wanted a home server that stored my books permanently, looked good, and synced with my phone, tablet, and Kindle without me having to think about it. I wanted all that for around $30. Here’s what I ended up with, and how it’s held up.”

item.title: Parrot
item.description: Spotted in my Calishat Snaps: From the help page: “Parrot is a web app for easily recording throwaway audio clips. It was originally intended for pronunciation practice but may find other uses.”

item.title: South Sudan Warns Against Disinformation Over Viral Bol Mel Document
item.description: Pan African Visions: “South Sudan’s justice authorities have dismissed a document circulating on social media that purports to be a leaked investigation implicating former Vice President Benjamin Bol Mel, calling it a fabrication and warning that it is part of a broader wave of disinformation targeting senior officials.”

item.title: Talkie Is a ‘Vintage LLM’ Trained on Pre-1930 Data to Help Facilitate ‘Time Travel’
item.description: Gizmodo: “In the case of Talkie, aka 13B 1930 LM, the cutoff is, as the name suggests, the year 1930. This choice of year might seem arbitrary, but it’s not: as we discussed here back in January, many forms of copyright expire on January 1 of the year that comes 95 years after the copyrighted material was released. This means that a whole lot of material released in 1930 went into the public domain at the start of this year.”

item.title: AI fails to make inroads with cybercriminals
item.description: University of Edinburgh: “Cybercriminals have been struggling to adopt AI in their work, reports the first of its kind study that analysed a dataset of 100 million posts from underground cybercrime communities.”

item.title: Children are drawing moustaches on their faces to fool online age checks – and it’s working
item.description: Euronews: “One mother told researchers she caught her son using an eyebrow pencil to draw a moustache on his face to pass a platform’s facial age estimation check. It worked. He was verified as 15. He was 12.”

item.title: A Maltese space research company wants to put a digital archive on the Moon
item.description: Times of Malta: “Spaceomix, founded by Prof Joseph Borg, is teaming up with Belgian space company Space Applications Services to place a solid-state data storage device called the ‘Lunar BioVault’ aboard the LUVMI-M lunar rover.”

item.title: We got to the bottom of the Sex and the City-style composting ads
item.description: New York Groove: “It’s hard to remember any recent conversation about transit ads that didn’t center around AI ‘companions,’ AI slop ‘recipes,’ endless GLP-1 plugs, and problematic tutorials on how to contour your nose…. So imagine my delight circa mid-March, when my texts and DMs started blowing up with pics of Scrappy, the surprisingly leggy mascot for city composting, recreating Carrie Bradshaw’s famous bus ad from the opening credits (and one pivotal first season episode) of Sex and the City.” Good morning, Internet…
